review.title: Choose a valid fluid-response assessment
fairness: Review-wide scope: all 11 new executable nodes were reviewed using candidate presentations, updates, exhibits, tasks, option labels and explanations, including preceding visible explanations. No rewritten, kept-unchanged or retired executable records were present. The one unkeyed individualized-pressure-target hold and eight remaining research gaps were noted but not scored. Review-only keys and author self-assessments were not evidence of quality.

Review-wide limitation: this is an offline editorial and clinical-plausibility review, with no network or independent current-guideline verification. PASS does not establish source validity or clinical approval; every draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified exam-frequency claims.

Passive leg raising with direct stroke-volume measurement is the best offered assessment. The resident must reject the apparently actionable pulse-pressure variation because of acquisition conditions, then choose a measurement strategy compatible with those conditions. The respiratory diameter surrogate is a credible neighboring error but less dependable here.

The options have parallel verbs and comparable specificity. Neither the diagnosis label atrial fibrillation nor the displayed 22% supplies the answer without knowing the measurement assumptions. Repetition of variation does not uniquely identify the key.

The complete task, named 56-year-old patient and short complaint are present. The finite presentation repeats the same clinical context. This first node requires no preceding answer. The consultation wording is understandable as review of ICU care rather than a new clinic treatment encounter.
suggestions: Retain both the rhythm and spontaneous-effort observations; do not remove necessary acquisition information in an attempt to make the item harder.

If acquisition detail is expanded, ensure the direct flow measurement is reliable despite beat-to-beat variability; do not imply that any isolated stroke-volume reading is sufficient in atrial fibrillation.

Across the five cases, optional presentation polish is to state explicitly that the named patient remains in the ICU and that the clinic consultation reviews the record. Preserve age, sex and short visit reason. Runtime wait displays and randomization were not demonstrated by this text-only review.

review.title: Separate fluid responsiveness from fluid tolerance
fairness: Increasing norepinephrine is the best offered next adjustment: marked hypotension persists despite substantial measured output, while the respiratory course deteriorated after fluid. The reversible stroke-volume rise is a genuine competing reason to consider fluid, so the learner must distinguish responsiveness from whether pursuing it is beneficial.

A positive passive-leg-raise response does not compel a bolus. Conversely, B-lines alone would not prove fluid-induced hydrostatic edema; the recommendation is supported by the combined oxygen trajectory, examination, flow and pressure findings. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming a proved edema mechanism.
Dobutamine is less compelling with vigorous contraction and substantial output. It is the weaker distractor, but the fluid-versus-pressor decision remains a consequential, credible comparison.

The preceding explanation teaches how to assess responsiveness, not whether this patient should receive fluid. The new respiratory and flow findings change the decision. The current update supplies norepinephrine use, and the current exhibit and shared presentation are sufficient without remembering the prior answer.
The task names the relevant decision dimensions without supplying their interpretation. Option labels are short and parallel; no nonmedical wording shortcut was identified.
suggestions: Retain the positive reversible flow response and post-fluid respiratory deterioration together; their tension is the useful learning objective.

Keep the conclusion patient-specific. Do not generalize this example into a rule that B-lines always prohibit fluid or that positive fluid responsiveness always requires fluid. Exact clinical ranking remains for clinician sign-off.

review.title: Start norepinephrine without waiting for central access

cues.phrase: Place a central line before starting norepinephrine / Start norepinephrine through the monitored upper-arm IV / Start epinephrine through the monitored upper-arm IV
cues.why: Component convergence selects the key without physiology: norepinephrine appears twice, the monitored upper-arm route appears twice, and only the key combines both repeated components. The three choices are an incomplete agent-by-route matrix.

cues.phrase: An upper-arm peripheral IV flushes freely and has a normal insertion site. Central-line preparation is under way.
cues.why: These are legitimate access observations, but in this option set they nearly narrate the route decision. Once combined with the convergence pattern, the perfusion and flow data add little discrimination.

fairness: Starting norepinephrine through the monitored proximal peripheral IV is the defensible best offered plan during severe ongoing hypoperfusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the stated explanation.

The current task already asks for an initial vasopressor delivery plan. The resident need not independently infer the need for pressure support, and the passive-leg-raise result does not distinguish the offered delivery plans. Choosing the familiar first-line drug and recalling that central access is not a prerequisite does not produce two consequential case-dependent steps here.
The initial node is self-contained, with age, sex, named patient and a complete task. The access information should not be withheld merely to obscure the key.
suggestions: Remove the incomplete component matrix. Prefer one narrow delivery decision with three clinically credible access plans, or use a balanced matrix only if all four combinations are genuinely plausible competitors; do not add a filler option just to complete the matrix.

For a resident application item, make actual access observations distinguish credible delivery plans while the perfusion findings determine the consequence of delay. Keep the access and monitoring requirements explicit and clinician-supported.
If retained as a basic safety item, seek explicit acceptance of that role and label it easy rather than claiming two-step resident difficulty.

review.title: Select an adjunct for persistent low pressure
clarityIssues: The update says 'Antimicrobial treatment and source control have been completed' during ongoing resuscitation. Completed antimicrobial treatment can mean the whole course has ended, rather than that initial antibiotics were administered. That creates avoidable uncertainty about elapsed time and current therapy.
fairness: Vasopressin is the defensible best offered adjunct for the described persistent low pressure and rising norepinephrine requirement. Epinephrine can be a legitimate vasoactive drug, but it is not equally preferred at the represented escalation stage; the explanation should not portray it as categorically contraindicated.

The options are parallel and no independent lexical giveaway was found. The weakness is the decision structure: the task asks for the additional drug after norepinephrine, while the exhibit supplies vigorous contraction, substantial output and a negative preload test. The key can be selected by a familiar escalation rule even if the flow and preload rows are removed.

The current norepinephrine dose and treatment interval are unspecified. I am not calling that alone a fatal fairness defect or inventing a threshold; however, 'successive ... increases' is a weak substitute for a concrete treatment trajectory if dose-dependent escalation is intended to be tested.

The node follows the peripheral-start node logically and repeats the current drug and pressure state. Apart from the ambiguous 'completed' wording, it stands alone with its shared presentation. Earlier feedback does not name vasopressin.
suggestions: Clarify whether the first antibiotic administration has finished and whether antibiotics continue; describe completed source control separately.

Make interpretation of a changing pressure/flow pattern alter the adjunct choice, rather than making the exhibit merely confirm a drug-sequence recall answer. Compare credible drugs at the same escalation stage.

If a dose or timing boundary is needed for the revised decision, obtain support for that exact boundary before adding it. Otherwise retain qualitative trajectory wording without pretending it creates a second inference.

review.title: Treat low flow despite restored arterial pressure
fairness: Dobutamine is the best offered adjustment. The learner must recognize that an acceptable arterial pressure has not restored perfusion, then select flow support in the presence of low cardiac index and newly weak contraction rather than simply escalating pressure or giving more fluid.

The current perfusion findings, cardiac index, echocardiographic change and absent preload response provide a coherent basis for ranking the options. The explanation appropriately says dobutamine is a supported option and calls for reassessment; it does not claim that all alternative inotropic strategies are prohibited.

The prior explanation supplies some scaffolding by distinguishing inadequate pressure from substantial output and by discussing absent fluid response. It does not state the present dobutamine answer. The new low-output phenotype reverses the earlier treatment rationale, so the sequence still requires application rather than literal recall of prior feedback.

All current pressures, drugs, perfusion findings and flow observations are present in this node. It can be answered with the shared presentation without remembering previous numbers. 'Later' makes the new cardiac findings temporally possible rather than contradicting the earlier vigorous contraction.
No label-length, wording-overlap or convergence shortcut was identified. The correct choice requires knowing what the observations mean and what the drugs do.
suggestions: Preserve the contrast between restored pressure and deteriorating perfusion, with measured low flow and a technically adequate preload assessment.

Repair the preceding node's ambiguous antimicrobial-course wording without adding a statement there that directly teaches when to choose dobutamine. Recheck this full sequence after any preceding-feedback revision.

review.title: Integrate persistent lactate elevation with improving perfusion
fairness: Maintaining the current MAP target is the best offered order. The learner must reconcile a still-elevated but falling lactate with improving bedside perfusion, then decide whether a further pressure or fluid intervention is justified.

The negative preload response weakens reflex volume loading; the improving examination and adequate current pressure weaken reflex target escalation. The explanation correctly leaves reassessment necessary rather than declaring the residual lactate harmless or proving a nonhypoperfusion cause.

The repeated 65 mm Hg value is necessary to compare maintaining versus changing the existing goal. It is not an unfair numeric match by itself: the main competing choice explicitly changes that goal, and the record must be interpreted to choose between them. The numerical labels do not create a convergent answer pattern.

The first node is self-contained with named age/sex, a short visit reason, a complete task and a coherent record. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally strong offered alternative was identified. This does not establish 65 mm Hg as the universal goal for all patients.
suggestions: Optional wording polish: replace 'on an unchanged norepinephrine target of 65 mm Hg' with a statement that the MAP goal is 65 mm Hg during norepinephrine treatment; the target is pressure, not drug dose.
Keep the falling trend and the actual bedside observations. Do not replace them with an authored conclusion that perfusion has normalized or teach that lactate can be disregarded.

review.title: Validate discordant arterial pressure before titration
clarityIssues: 'The arterial pressure system has no fluid-filled zero line' is specialized setup language without an explanation of the system being described. A resident may confuse the zero-reference arrangement with the fluid-filled arterial pressure tubing itself.

The task asks 'Which assessment', but the key is an equipment correction, while the other two choices obtain new physiological measurements. A neutral next-action task or a same-stage troubleshooting option set would be clearer.

cues.phrase: Its transducer is now above the level of the right atrium / Relevel the arterial-pressure transducer to the right atrium
cues.why: The exhibit names the misplaced object and reference point; only the key repeats both and reverses the stated setup problem. A reader can match problem to correction without interpreting the pressure discrepancy.

cues.phrase: after the bed and monitoring equipment were repositioned
cues.why: This primes equipment trouble before the table; combined with the explicit transducer position, it makes the unrelated echo and venous-saturation measurements weak competitors. The chronology is legitimate, but the current choices do not test its interpretation.

fairness: For the described conventional hydrostatic arrangement, a transducer above the right atrial reference can read falsely low. Releveling and reassessment are the best offered action. No confident reversal of the physiological rule was found.

The cuff/arterial discrepancy and unchanged examination support checking measurement validity, but the stem then supplies the exact hardware error. Recognizing the already-described error and choosing its literal correction is not two independent consequential steps.

The follow-up coherently tests a different problem after the earlier target decision. Its current cuff readings and equipment findings suffice without the preceding answer. The exact capillary-refill value and alert mental status are only in the earlier node; if strict isolated display is intended, repeat those observations concisely rather than saying merely 'remain unchanged'.
suggestions: Describe the pressure setup in ordinary, unambiguous terms, retaining the physical facts required for the hydrostatic interpretation.

Compare plausible troubleshooting or immediate management actions at the same decision stage, with waveform, reference-level and repeat-pressure observations that actually distinguish them. Do not simply hide the needed transducer position.
Alternatively, retain this as an explicitly accepted basic measurement-safety item. Do not describe the present matching task as hard clinical reasoning.

review.title: Do not defer empirical antibiotics for a low biomarker
clarityIssues: 'After a focused diagnostic reassessment' does not specify what is reassessed or whether it introduces any meaningful delay. A rapid reassessment can occur during the current resuscitation, so the temporal alternatives are not clearly exclusive.

cues.phrase: begin the planned empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotic treatment
cues.why: 'Planned' preannounces that the treatment decision has already been made. 'Empirical' also makes waiting for organism identification sound internally inconsistent before the learner interprets infection evidence or procalcitonin.

cues.phrase: After the initial culture identification / During the current shock resuscitation
cues.why: The option set contrasts waiting for a stated pending result with the sole immediate option in an explicitly urgent shock frame. The low biomarker can be ignored and the familiar urgency rule still selects the key.

fairness: Starting empirical antibiotics during current resuscitation is clinically defensible given the infection findings, hypotension and already obtained samples. A procalcitonin result within the reference interval does not reliably exclude the need for treatment in this setting.

The vague reassessment option is the fairness problem: it can overlap with prompt treatment, rather than represent a clearly different management decision. This is repairable wording and option design, not evidence that delayed antibiotics are equally appropriate.

The presentation is short, patient-specific and self-contained. The explanation communicates the useful principle, but the current item tests one timing rule, not two consequential inferences. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: Remove 'planned' and ask a neutral, complete management task. State the actual reassessment action if it remains an option and make its relationship to starting treatment unambiguous without inventing a fixed delay.
Use a credible competing interpretation of the supplied evidence if a resident application item is desired; do not simply make infection less certain while leaving an unsupported key.
If the objective is the basic safety rule that a low procalcitonin must not delay treatment of likely infection with shock, seek explicit basic-item acceptance and keep the item short.

review.title: Time source control during ongoing resuscitation

cues.phrase: The surgical and interventional-radiology teams have agreed on drainage / the agreed drainage procedure
cues.why: The indication and procedure are settled twice. In this option set, the learner is left choosing the plainly indicated intervention against two complete-recovery delays, rather than resolving a remaining procedural decision.

cues.phrase: Schedule drainage after vasopressors have been discontinued / Schedule drainage after lactate reaches the reference interval / Proceed with drainage during the ongoing resuscitation
cues.why: Two options demand complete resolution of a current abnormality, while the key is the only concurrent action and repeats the task's resuscitation language. This wait/wait/proceed structure provides an urgency shortcut.

fairness: Proceeding with drainage during ongoing resuscitation is the best offered plan. The explanation appropriately includes procedural safety assessment and does not require complete lactate normalization or vasopressor discontinuation.

The physiological observations do not distinguish close competing plans: either complete-recovery delay remains inferior over a broad range of the supplied values. Removing the lactate number and exact MAP does not change the answer. This is one source-control timing rule, not a two-step decision.

The sequence is coherent: antibiotics have begun, CT localizes a collection, and a drainage approach is agreed. The update supplies enough current information to answer independently. Earlier feedback's instruction to treat infection during resuscitation further rehearses the concurrent-treatment pattern, though it does not literally name drainage.
No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The procedure's exact technical approach need not be invented because this task explicitly concerns timing.
suggestions: Replace the two unsupported complete-recovery prerequisites with credible plans addressing an actual, explicitly described remaining safety or sequencing issue. Keep source control urgent and obtain evidence for any proposed procedural constraint.

Do not add an arbitrary waiting interval, drug threshold or organ-specific procedure comparison simply to create difficulty. If no genuine competing decision fits this objective, retain it only through explicit acceptance as a basic safety item.
Remove duplicate statements that the drainage decision is agreed while retaining enough context to keep the task about timing rather than indication.

review.title: Choose the initial reassessment of persistent shock

cues.phrase: Obtain bedside transthoracic echocardiography
cues.why: Only this investigation is explicitly described as bedside, giving it a portability advantage in an unstable-patient vignette. This is a partial wording cue, not proof by itself: a pulmonary artery catheter can also be placed at the bedside.

fairness: Bedside echocardiography is the best offered first investigation. Persistent severe hypotension with elevated filling pressure and absent response to a monitored bolus warrants reassessment for cardiac or obstructive contributions. Immediate transport for targeted CT is less attractive, and an invasive catheter does not substitute for structural assessment.

The main weakness is the deletion test. The same first-echo answer follows from undifferentiated persistent severe shock even without the neck-vein, narrow-pulse-pressure and filling-pressure details. Those findings suggest a mechanism, but interpreting that mechanism is not necessary to select among the current options.

The postoperative context makes embolism a credible possibility, but the options primarily distinguish a familiar first-line test from a targeted transfer investigation and an invasive later investigation. This remains easy for the intended resident audience.
The first node is self-contained, its task is complete and the explanation does not overstate a definite obstructive diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: To require two consequential steps, supply an actual limitation or result of the initial assessment and ask for the next investigation that resolves the remaining physiological question. Give enough acquisition information to distinguish repeat or alternative imaging from advanced hemodynamic measurement or CT.
Keep option descriptions comparable in setting and specificity; do not use 'bedside' only to advertise the preferred test's feasibility.
If this remains an initial-echo recognition item, label and obtain acceptance of that basic role. Do not raise apparent difficulty by adding more classic shock findings that do not affect the choice.

review.title: Respond to pericardial compression during persistent shock
clarityIssues: The option commits to 'Arrange urgent pericardial drainage', whereas the explanation repeatedly softens this to 'drainage assessment'. In the stated shock context, distinguish prompt mobilization for drainage and selection of its approach from merely requesting another assessment.

cues.phrase: Pericardial fluid / Arrange urgent pericardial drainage

cues.phrase: Which immediate intervention / Arrange urgent pericardial drainage
cues.why: Only the key includes an urgency adjective that mirrors 'immediate'. The other actions could also be initiated immediately, so this label adds a preferential wording signal rather than clinical information.

fairness: Urgent drainage is the best offered priority given persistent shock, pericardial fluid and right-sided chamber collapse. Escalating norepinephrine may be temporizing support but does not address the represented filling impediment; the task's priority wording makes it less appropriate than drainage. Dobutamine lacks support from the preserved-contraction findings.

The explanation is clinically plausible when read together with the shock context. Chamber collapse should not be taught as an isolated universal indication for drainage regardless of clinical findings. I am not asserting that the stated patient lacks a drainage indication.

The similar-size comparison is intended to challenge reliance on collection size, but removing the entire Yesterday column leaves the same obvious drainage answer. Neither distractor actually requires interpreting the unchanged size. A classic collapse-to-drainage association, with one clearly weaker inotrope distractor, does not establish two consequential steps.

The sequence follows logically from the prior echo choice, and the current MAP, treatment and echo findings permit a standalone answer with the shared presentation. The earlier feedback points toward cardiac or obstructive causes but does not explicitly teach drainage. The newly revealed prior study is not a contradiction, although its timing would be clearer if introduced as a comparison report.
suggestions: Align the explanation with urgent mobilization for drainage while leaving the exact approach dependent on the collection and clinical setting.

Remove key-only urgency wording and reconsider the two generic infusion foils. Any stronger procedural or temporizing alternatives need patient-specific findings that establish one best priority; do not invent anatomy, thresholds or contraindications.

inputCues.phrase: An upper-arm peripheral IV flushes freely and has a normal insertion site. Central-line preparation is under way.
inputCues.why: These are legitimate access observations, but in this option set they nearly narrate the route decision. Once combined with the convergence pattern, the perfusion and flow data add little discrimination.

inputFairness: Starting norepinephrine through the monitored proximal peripheral IV is the defensible best offered plan during severe ongoing hypoperfusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the stated explanation.

The current task already asks for an initial vasopressor delivery plan. The resident need not independently infer the need for pressure support, and the passive-leg-raise result does not distinguish the offered delivery plans. Choosing the familiar first-line drug and recalling that central access is not a prerequisite does not produce two consequential case-dependent steps here.
The initial node is self-contained, with age, sex, named patient and a complete task. The access information should not be withheld merely to obscure the key.
inputSuggestions: Remove the incomplete component matrix. Prefer one narrow delivery decision with three clinically credible access plans, or use a balanced matrix only if all four combinations are genuinely plausible competitors; do not add a filler option just to complete the matrix.

For a resident application item, make actual access observations distinguish credible delivery plans while the perfusion findings determine the consequence of delay. Keep the access and monitoring requirements explicit and clinician-supported.
If retained as a basic safety item, seek explicit acceptance of that role and label it easy rather than claiming two-step resident difficulty.

inputClarityIssues: The update says 'Antimicrobial treatment and source control have been completed' during ongoing resuscitation. Completed antimicrobial treatment can mean the whole course has ended, rather than that initial antibiotics were administered. That creates avoidable uncertainty about elapsed time and current therapy.
inputFairness: Vasopressin is the defensible best offered adjunct for the described persistent low pressure and rising norepinephrine requirement. Epinephrine can be a legitimate vasoactive drug, but it is not equally preferred at the represented escalation stage; the explanation should not portray it as categorically contraindicated.

The options are parallel and no independent lexical giveaway was found. The weakness is the decision structure: the task asks for the additional drug after norepinephrine, while the exhibit supplies vigorous contraction, substantial output and a negative preload test. The key can be selected by a familiar escalation rule even if the flow and preload rows are removed.

The current norepinephrine dose and treatment interval are unspecified. I am not calling that alone a fatal fairness defect or inventing a threshold; however, 'successive ... increases' is a weak substitute for a concrete treatment trajectory if dose-dependent escalation is intended to be tested.

The node follows the peripheral-start node logically and repeats the current drug and pressure state. Apart from the ambiguous 'completed' wording, it stands alone with its shared presentation. Earlier feedback does not name vasopressin.
inputSuggestions: Clarify whether the first antibiotic administration has finished and whether antibiotics continue; describe completed source control separately.

Make interpretation of a changing pressure/flow pattern alter the adjunct choice, rather than making the exhibit merely confirm a drug-sequence recall answer. Compare credible drugs at the same escalation stage.

If a dose or timing boundary is needed for the revised decision, obtain support for that exact boundary before adding it. Otherwise retain qualitative trajectory wording without pretending it creates a second inference.
attempts.repair: Clarified ongoing antibiotic treatment and separately completed source control. Replaced the drug-sequence lead-in and epinephrine option with a neutral adjustment task and a real fluid competitor. The data are now needed to rank the three mechanisms.
attempts.resolution: Antibiotics explicitly continue and the source-control procedure is separately complete. The neutral task compares pressure, volume and inotropic adjustments. Direct output and raw reversible measurements are required to choose among them. Qualitative norepinephrine escalation carries no invented dose boundary.
attempts.remainingIssue: Clinical circumstances can support other vasopressors. The item makes a patient-specific comparison of the offered actions and claims no universal dose boundary.
attempts.finalDisposition: Clarified ongoing antibiotic treatment and separately completed source control. Replaced the drug-sequence lead-in and epinephrine option with a neutral adjustment task and a real fluid competitor. The data are now needed to rank the three mechanisms.

inputClarityIssues: 'The arterial pressure system has no fluid-filled zero line' is specialized setup language without an explanation of the system being described. A resident may confuse the zero-reference arrangement with the fluid-filled arterial pressure tubing itself.

The task asks 'Which assessment', but the key is an equipment correction, while the other two choices obtain new physiological measurements. A neutral next-action task or a same-stage troubleshooting option set would be clearer.

inputCues.phrase: Its transducer is now above the level of the right atrium / Relevel the arterial-pressure transducer to the right atrium
inputCues.why: The exhibit names the misplaced object and reference point; only the key repeats both and reverses the stated setup problem. A reader can match problem to correction without interpreting the pressure discrepancy.

inputCues.phrase: after the bed and monitoring equipment were repositioned
inputCues.why: This primes equipment trouble before the table; combined with the explicit transducer position, it makes the unrelated echo and venous-saturation measurements weak competitors. The chronology is legitimate, but the current choices do not test its interpretation.

inputFairness: For the described conventional hydrostatic arrangement, a transducer above the right atrial reference can read falsely low. Releveling and reassessment are the best offered action. No confident reversal of the physiological rule was found.

The cuff/arterial discrepancy and unchanged examination support checking measurement validity, but the stem then supplies the exact hardware error. Recognizing the already-described error and choosing its literal correction is not two independent consequential steps.

The follow-up coherently tests a different problem after the earlier target decision. Its current cuff readings and equipment findings suffice without the preceding answer. The exact capillary-refill value and alert mental status are only in the earlier node; if strict isolated display is intended, repeat those observations concisely rather than saying merely 'remain unchanged'.
inputSuggestions: Describe the pressure setup in ordinary, unambiguous terms, retaining the physical facts required for the hydrostatic interpretation.

Compare plausible troubleshooting or immediate management actions at the same decision stage, with waveform, reference-level and repeat-pressure observations that actually distinguish them. Do not simply hide the needed transducer position.
Alternatively, retain this as an explicitly accepted basic measurement-safety item. Do not describe the present matching task as hard clinical reasoning.

attempts.resolution: Ordinary tubing description replaces unexplained zero-line shorthand. All options are pressure-system actions. attempts.remainingIssue: A resident familiar with transducer physics may solve it quickly. It is retained as a fair moderate acquisition problem after removing the literal problem-to-correction matching set.
attempts.finalDisposition: Explained the system in ordinary language, replaced the assessment lead-in with an action task and replaced unrelated physiological tests with three plausible troubleshooting actions. Raw heights replace an authored statement naming the setup fault.

inputClarityIssues: 'After a focused diagnostic reassessment' does not specify what is reassessed or whether it introduces any meaningful delay. A rapid reassessment can occur during the current resuscitation, so the temporal alternatives are not clearly exclusive.

inputCues.phrase: begin the planned empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotic treatment
inputCues.why: 'Planned' preannounces that the treatment decision has already been made. 'Empirical' also makes waiting for organism identification sound internally inconsistent before the learner interprets infection evidence or procalcitonin.

inputCues.phrase: After the initial culture identification / During the current shock resuscitation
inputCues.why: The option set contrasts waiting for a stated pending result with the sole immediate option in an explicitly urgent shock frame. The low biomarker can be ignored and the familiar urgency rule still selects the key.

inputFairness: Starting empirical antibiotics during current resuscitation is clinically defensible given the infection findings, hypotension and already obtained samples. A procalcitonin result within the reference interval does not reliably exclude the need for treatment in this setting.

The vague reassessment option is the fairness problem: it can overlap with prompt treatment, rather than represent a clearly different management decision. This is repairable wording and option design, not evidence that delayed antibiotics are equally appropriate.

Use a credible competing interpretation of the supplied evidence if a resident application item is desired; do not simply make infection less certain while leaving an unsupported key.

inputCues.phrase: The surgical and interventional-radiology teams have agreed on drainage / the agreed drainage procedure
inputCues.why: The indication and procedure are settled twice. In this option set, the learner is left choosing the plainly indicated intervention against two complete-recovery delays, rather than resolving a remaining procedural decision.

inputCues.phrase: Schedule drainage after vasopressors have been discontinued / Schedule drainage after lactate reaches the reference interval / Proceed with drainage during the ongoing resuscitation
inputCues.why: Two options demand complete resolution of a current abnormality, while the key is the only concurrent action and repeats the task's resuscitation language. This wait/wait/proceed structure provides an urgency shortcut.

inputFairness: Proceeding with drainage during ongoing resuscitation is the best offered plan. The explanation appropriately includes procedural safety assessment and does not require complete lactate normalization or vasopressor discontinuation.

The physiological observations do not distinguish close competing plans: either complete-recovery delay remains inferior over a broad range of the supplied values. Removing the lactate number and exact MAP does not change the answer. This is one source-control timing rule, not a two-step decision.

The sequence is coherent: antibiotics have begun, CT localizes a collection, and a drainage approach is agreed. The update supplies enough current information to answer independently. Earlier feedback's instruction to treat infection during resuscitation further rehearses the concurrent-treatment pattern, though it does not literally name drainage.
No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The procedure's exact technical approach need not be invented because this task explicitly concerns timing.
inputSuggestions: Replace the two unsupported complete-recovery prerequisites with credible plans addressing an actual, explicitly described remaining safety or sequencing issue. Keep source control urgent and obtain evidence for any proposed procedural constraint.

Do not add an arbitrary waiting interval, drug threshold or organ-specific procedure comparison simply to create difficulty. If no genuine competing decision fits this objective, retain it only through explicit acceptance as a basic safety item.
Remove duplicate statements that the drainage decision is agreed while retaining enough context to keep the task about timing rather than indication.
attempts.repair: Removed duplicate declarations that drainage was agreed and replaced the complete-recovery prerequisites with narrower care plans. Re-solved the timing set against the actual supported pressure and source-control need.
attempts.resolution: The revised stabilization plan has no represented unresolved safety issue, and its duration is undefined. Adding one would require a new exact procedural constraint and supporting evidence. The remaining set still permits an urgency shortcut.

attempts.finalDisposition: The one attempted repair did not establish a fair moderate comparison. Unsupported delay or procedural criteria would introduce a fairness problem, so the item is parked.

inputCues.phrase: Obtain bedside transthoracic echocardiography
inputCues.why: Only this investigation is explicitly described as bedside, giving it a portability advantage in an unstable-patient vignette. This is a partial wording cue, not proof by itself: a pulmonary artery catheter can also be placed at the bedside.

inputFairness: Bedside echocardiography is the best offered first investigation. Persistent severe hypotension with elevated filling pressure and absent response to a monitored bolus warrants reassessment for cardiac or obstructive contributions. Immediate transport for targeted CT is less attractive, and an invasive catheter does not substitute for structural assessment.

The main weakness is the deletion test. The same first-echo answer follows from undifferentiated persistent severe shock even without the neck-vein, narrow-pulse-pressure and filling-pressure details. Those findings suggest a mechanism, but interpreting that mechanism is not necessary to select among the current options.

The postoperative context makes embolism a credible possibility, but the options primarily distinguish a familiar first-line test from a targeted transfer investigation and an invasive later investigation. This remains easy for the intended resident audience.
The first node is self-contained, its task is complete and the explanation does not overstate a definite obstructive diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
inputSuggestions: To require two consequential steps, supply an actual limitation or result of the initial assessment and ask for the next investigation that resolves the remaining physiological question. Give enough acquisition information to distinguish repeat or alternative imaging from advanced hemodynamic measurement or CT.
Keep option descriptions comparable in setting and specificity; do not use 'bedside' only to advertise the preferred test's feasibility.
If this remains an initial-echo recognition item, label and obtain acceptance of that basic role. Do not raise apparent difficulty by adding more classic shock findings that do not affect the choice.

inputReview.title: Choose a valid fluid-response assessment
fairness: Review-wide scope: all 11 new executable nodes were reviewed using candidate presentations, updates, exhibits, tasks, option labels and explanations, including preceding visible explanations. No rewritten, kept-unchanged or retired executable records were present. The one unkeyed individualized-pressure-target hold and eight remaining research gaps were noted but not scored. Review-only keys and author self-assessments were not evidence of quality.

Review-wide limitation: this is an offline editorial and clinical-plausibility review, with no network or independent current-guideline verification. PASS does not establish source validity or clinical approval; every draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified exam-frequency claims.

Passive leg raising with direct stroke-volume measurement is the best offered assessment. The resident must reject the apparently actionable pulse-pressure variation because of acquisition conditions, then choose a measurement strategy compatible with those conditions. The respiratory diameter surrogate is a credible neighboring error but less dependable here.

The options have parallel verbs and comparable specificity. Neither the diagnosis label atrial fibrillation nor the displayed 22% supplies the answer without knowing the measurement assumptions. Repetition of variation does not uniquely identify the key.

The complete task, named 56-year-old patient and short complaint are present. The finite presentation repeats the same clinical context. This first node requires no preceding answer. The consultation wording is understandable as review of ICU care rather than a new clinic treatment encounter.
suggestions: Retain both the rhythm and spontaneous-effort observations; do not remove necessary acquisition information in an attempt to make the item harder.

If acquisition detail is expanded, ensure the direct flow measurement is reliable despite beat-to-beat variability; do not imply that any isolated stroke-volume reading is sufficient in atrial fibrillation.

Across the five cases, optional presentation polish is to state explicitly that the named patient remains in the ICU and that the clinic consultation reviews the record. Preserve age, sex and short visit reason. Runtime wait displays and randomization were not demonstrated by this text-only review.

answerChoices.label: Track pulse-pressure variation from the arterial waveform
answerChoices.rationale: Both the irregular rhythm and spontaneous breaths disturb the cyclic relationship needed to interpret this displayed value. A large number does not establish fluid responsiveness under these conditions.

answerChoices.rationale: A reversible change in preload can be assessed through direct flow measurement despite the represented breathing pattern and rhythm. The later treatment decision still requires assessment of perfusion need and fluid risk.

answerChoices.rationale: Inspiratory effort and other cardiopulmonary factors affect vena-caval variation. It is less dependable for this decision than a direct reversible flow-response test.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Covered the keyed row and checked the task for 'stroke volume' or 'leg raising'. Neither appears there. All three choices are seven or eight words and describe bedside measurements. The monitor value tempts the near-miss. No option carries explanatory qualifiers or a uniquely comprehensive plan.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: All choices assess responsiveness before deciding on further fluid. None commits the learner to a treatment or an unrelated diagnostic pathway.
twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize that the displayed variation combines an irregular rhythm with patient-triggered breaths and cannot be interpreted as a reliable preload test.
Choose a reversible maneuver with direct flow measurement that remains usable in those conditions.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate for PGY-2/3. The error is trusting a numerical dynamic index while missing two acquisition limitations.
authorGate.singleBestAnswer: Direct flow during PLR accommodates the represented rhythm and breathing. The competing respiratory indices do not have valid acquisition conditions here.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Variable R-R intervals and spontaneous patient-triggered ventilation occur together.
authorGate.residentErrorConsequence: A false-positive interpretation could prompt ineffective volume loading.

inputReview.title: Separate fluid responsiveness from fluid tolerance
fairness: Increasing norepinephrine is the best offered next adjustment: marked hypotension persists despite substantial measured output, while the respiratory course deteriorated after fluid. The reversible stroke-volume rise is a genuine competing reason to consider fluid, so the learner must distinguish responsiveness from whether pursuing it is beneficial.

A positive passive-leg-raise response does not compel a bolus. Conversely, B-lines alone would not prove fluid-induced hydrostatic edema; the recommendation is supported by the combined oxygen trajectory, examination, flow and pressure findings. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming a proved edema mechanism.
Dobutamine is less compelling with vigorous contraction and substantial output. It is the weaker distractor, but the fluid-versus-pressor decision remains a consequential, credible comparison.

The preceding explanation teaches how to assess responsiveness, not whether this patient should receive fluid. The new respiratory and flow findings change the decision. The current update supplies norepinephrine use, and the current exhibit and shared presentation are sufficient without remembering the prior answer.
The task names the relevant decision dimensions without supplying their interpretation. Option labels are short and parallel; no nonmedical wording shortcut was identified.
suggestions: Retain the positive reversible flow response and post-fluid respiratory deterioration together; their tension is the useful learning objective.

Keep the conclusion patient-specific. Do not generalize this example into a rule that B-lines always prohibit fluid or that positive fluid responsiveness always requires fluid. Exact clinical ranking remains for clinician sign-off.

authorGate.coverTheKey: The task names three data domains that every plan must fit. All labels name one specific infusion adjustment and contain five words. No label includes a rationale, cautious information-gathering or availability permission. The conspicuous positive response deliberately favors the closest wrong plan until fluid risk is interpreted.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three immediate hemodynamic infusion adjustments at the same reassessment stage.
twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the reversible stroke-volume rise as a real preload response and the oxygen/crackle/B-line trajectory as substantial fluid risk.
Treat the persistent hypotension through norepinephrine titration given vigorous contraction and substantial output.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted hard for PGY-2/3 because the correct preload interpretation does not directly select the fluid action.
authorGate.singleBestAnswer: Pressure is inadequate, contraction/output are substantial, and further fluid has an unfavorable current respiratory tradeoff. Review must assess whether these observations sufficiently rank pressor titration over a small monitored bolus.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Respiratory deterioration followed the preceding fluid while current cardiac contraction and output remain substantial.
authorGate.residentErrorConsequence: Pursuing every positive preload test can worsen lung fluid burden without resolving the dominant pressure deficit safely.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the respiratory trajectory and the bolus becomes a reasonable competitor. Delete the flow-test values and the tempting positive-test inference disappears. Each exhibit row affects a different boundary.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace respiratory deterioration with stable oxygenation and substantial ongoing gastrointestinal volume loss while retaining impaired perfusion and the reversible flow rise. A monitored balanced-crystalloid challenge becomes the preferred offered adjustment.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Prior feedback establishes the valid test method. It does not reveal the new respiratory trajectory or make the treatment decision. The later node scores fluid risk and need, with a distinct concept ID.
authorGate.residualConcern: This is an individualized treatment ranking. Melissa must assess the exact respiratory evidence, output measurements and plausibility of the competing bolus before exact acceptance.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a fourth vasopressin option that could overlap with norepinephrine escalation before an escalation trajectory is supplied. Re-solved the three remaining actions against the current chart.

observationClassification.numericBoundary: Patient readings and chronology are constructed observations. The 65 mm Hg initial target is source-supported. No constructed number is a new treatment threshold, probability, drug regimen, testing duration or demographic weight.

choices.rationale: The flow response is genuine, but it does not establish that another bolus offers the best risk-benefit balance. Worsening oxygen needs and new diffuse lung findings after fluids argue against further empiric volume loading here.
choices.temptation: Treat a positive PLR result as an instruction to give fluid.
choices.reasonableCounterfactual: The same preload response with impaired perfusion, substantial ongoing volume loss and adequate respiratory tolerance would support a monitored crystalloid challenge.

choices.rationale: The represented low pressure occurs with vigorous contraction and substantial measured output. There is no demonstrated low-output cardiac dysfunction to make an inotrope the preferred adjustment.
choices.temptation: Use persistent hypoperfusion as an inotrope indication without checking the flow and ventricular findings.
choices.reasonableCounterfactual: Persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac systolic dysfunction and low flow after appropriate volume and arterial-pressure assessment.

choices.temptation: Integrate the positive response with current output and fluid-related risk.
choices.reasonableCounterfactual: This current hypotensive, fluid-intolerant context with preserved contraction.

inputReview.title: Start norepinephrine without waiting for central access

cues.phrase: Place a central line before starting norepinephrine / Start norepinephrine through the monitored upper-arm IV / Start epinephrine through the monitored upper-arm IV
cues.why: Component convergence selects the key without physiology: norepinephrine appears twice, the monitored upper-arm route appears twice, and only the key combines both repeated components. The three choices are an incomplete agent-by-route matrix.

cues.phrase: An upper-arm peripheral IV flushes freely and has a normal insertion site. Central-line preparation is under way.
cues.why: These are legitimate access observations, but in this option set they nearly narrate the route decision. Once combined with the convergence pattern, the perfusion and flow data add little discrimination.

fairness: Starting norepinephrine through the monitored proximal peripheral IV is the defensible best offered plan during severe ongoing hypoperfusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the stated explanation.

The current task already asks for an initial vasopressor delivery plan. The resident need not independently infer the need for pressure support, and the passive-leg-raise result does not distinguish the offered delivery plans. Choosing the familiar first-line drug and recalling that central access is not a prerequisite does not produce two consequential case-dependent steps here.
The initial node is self-contained, with age, sex, named patient and a complete task. The access information should not be withheld merely to obscure the key.
suggestions: Remove the incomplete component matrix. Prefer one narrow delivery decision with three clinically credible access plans, or use a balanced matrix only if all four combinations are genuinely plausible competitors; do not add a filler option just to complete the matrix.

For a resident application item, make actual access observations distinguish credible delivery plans while the perfusion findings determine the consequence of delay. Keep the access and monitoring requirements explicit and clinician-supported.
If retained as a basic safety item, seek explicit acceptance of that role and label it easy rather than claiming two-step resident difficulty.

inputReview.title: Select an adjunct for persistent low pressure
clarityIssues: The update says 'Antimicrobial treatment and source control have been completed' during ongoing resuscitation. Completed antimicrobial treatment can mean the whole course has ended, rather than that initial antibiotics were administered. That creates avoidable uncertainty about elapsed time and current therapy.
fairness: Vasopressin is the defensible best offered adjunct for the described persistent low pressure and rising norepinephrine requirement. Epinephrine can be a legitimate vasoactive drug, but it is not equally preferred at the represented escalation stage; the explanation should not portray it as categorically contraindicated.

The options are parallel and no independent lexical giveaway was found. The weakness is the decision structure: the task asks for the additional drug after norepinephrine, while the exhibit supplies vigorous contraction, substantial output and a negative preload test. The key can be selected by a familiar escalation rule even if the flow and preload rows are removed.

The current norepinephrine dose and treatment interval are unspecified. I am not calling that alone a fatal fairness defect or inventing a threshold; however, 'successive ... increases' is a weak substitute for a concrete treatment trajectory if dose-dependent escalation is intended to be tested.

The node follows the peripheral-start node logically and repeats the current drug and pressure state. Apart from the ambiguous 'completed' wording, it stands alone with its shared presentation. Earlier feedback does not name vasopressin.
suggestions: Clarify whether the first antibiotic administration has finished and whether antibiotics continue; describe completed source control separately.

Make interpretation of a changing pressure/flow pattern alter the adjunct choice, rather than making the exhibit merely confirm a drug-sequence recall answer. Compare credible drugs at the same escalation stage.

If a dose or timing boundary is needed for the revised decision, obtain support for that exact boundary before adding it. Otherwise retain qualitative trajectory wording without pretending it creates a second inference.

inputReview.title: Treat low flow despite restored arterial pressure
fairness: Dobutamine is the best offered adjustment. The learner must recognize that an acceptable arterial pressure has not restored perfusion, then select flow support in the presence of low cardiac index and newly weak contraction rather than simply escalating pressure or giving more fluid.

The current perfusion findings, cardiac index, echocardiographic change and absent preload response provide a coherent basis for ranking the options. The explanation appropriately says dobutamine is a supported option and calls for reassessment; it does not claim that all alternative inotropic strategies are prohibited.

The prior explanation supplies some scaffolding by distinguishing inadequate pressure from substantial output and by discussing absent fluid response. It does not state the present dobutamine answer. The new low-output phenotype reverses the earlier treatment rationale, so the sequence still requires application rather than literal recall of prior feedback.

All current pressures, drugs, perfusion findings and flow observations are present in this node. It can be answered with the shared presentation without remembering previous numbers. 'Later' makes the new cardiac findings temporally possible rather than contradicting the earlier vigorous contraction.
No label-length, wording-overlap or convergence shortcut was identified. The correct choice requires knowing what the observations mean and what the drugs do.
suggestions: Preserve the contrast between restored pressure and deteriorating perfusion, with measured low flow and a technically adequate preload assessment.

Repair the preceding node's ambiguous antimicrobial-course wording without adding a statement there that directly teaches when to choose dobutamine. Recheck this full sequence after any preceding-feedback revision.

answerChoices.label: Start norepinephrine through the monitored upper-arm IV

answerChoices.label: Start epinephrine through the monitored upper-arm IV
answerChoices.rationale: The access route addresses urgency, but norepinephrine is the preferred initial agent for the represented septic shock with preserved contraction. Epinephrine is a credible agent in other hemodynamic contexts.

authorGate.coverTheKey: All labels are four or five words and name one infusion adjustment. The task uses hypoperfusion without specifying a contractility treatment. The key carries no extra monitoring or safety phrase. The data identify a mechanism without naming a cardiomyopathy diagnosis.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Immediate infusion adjustment after pressure, flow and preload reassessment. Epinephrine is omitted because it is another guideline-supported cardiac-support strategy.
twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize the new low-output cardiac pattern from measured index, changed contraction and peripheral findings despite MAP recovery.
Add inotropic support after confirming that neither more pressure nor an empiric volume load addresses the represented limitation.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted hard. The learner must abandon the earlier preserved-output phenotype and avoid equating restored MAP with completed resuscitation.
authorGate.singleBestAnswer: The represented pressure, direct flow and response assessment support the dobutamine option. Another supported inotrope strategy is deliberately outside this single-best set.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The achieved MAP coexists with newly low measured flow and weak contraction.
authorGate.residentErrorConsequence: Further pressure-directed escalation can leave the low-output mechanism and organ hypoperfusion insufficiently addressed.
authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the new flow/contraction row and the precise reason for dobutamine is absent. Remove the pressure row and the task no longer establishes that pressure support is adequate before the inotrope comparison.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace the current MAP with persistent inadequate pressure and restore vigorous contraction and substantial output. Norepinephrine titration becomes the best offered adjustment.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: The previous dobutamine distractor said the earlier phenotype lacked low-output dysfunction. This creates some legitimate scaffolding. The new node earns a changed decision through fresh contrary flow, contraction and perfusion findings. Independent review must inspect that full sequence.
authorGate.residualConcern: Low-certainty intervention evidence and paired-sequence scaffolding remain explicit. No mortality benefit or forced universal inotrope protocol is claimed.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed an epinephrine alternative that would create a second supported key. Retained pressure escalation as the clinically plausible anchor after the previous node.

inputReview.title: Integrate persistent lactate elevation with improving perfusion
fairness: Maintaining the current MAP target is the best offered order. The learner must reconcile a still-elevated but falling lactate with improving bedside perfusion, then decide whether a further pressure or fluid intervention is justified.

The negative preload response weakens reflex volume loading; the improving examination and adequate current pressure weaken reflex target escalation. The explanation correctly leaves reassessment necessary rather than declaring the residual lactate harmless or proving a nonhypoperfusion cause.

The repeated 65 mm Hg value is necessary to compare maintaining versus changing the existing goal. It is not an unfair numeric match by itself: the main competing choice explicitly changes that goal, and the record must be interpreted to choose between them. The numerical labels do not create a convergent answer pattern.

The first node is self-contained with named age/sex, a short visit reason, a complete task and a coherent record. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally strong offered alternative was identified. This does not establish 65 mm Hg as the universal goal for all patients.
suggestions: Optional wording polish: replace 'on an unchanged norepinephrine target of 65 mm Hg' with a statement that the MAP goal is 65 mm Hg during norepinephrine treatment; the target is pressure, not drug dose.
Keep the falling trend and the actual bedside observations. Do not replace them with an authored conclusion that perfusion has normalized or teach that lactate can be disregarded.

authorGate.coverTheKey: The key and pressure distractor share identical structure and differ by the target. The fluid plan has comparable specificity. No option alone promises to monitor carefully. The complaint and task do not tell the learner that lactate is misleading or that resuscitation is complete.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three current resuscitation orders. Serial observation is shared background care, with no diagnostic-test choice hidden in the key.
twoConsequentialSteps: Reconcile residual hyperlactatemia with a falling trend, improving peripheral and organ signs, and absent preload response.
Maintain the current supported pressure target while following serial findings instead of prescribing an unsubstantiated escalation.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate to hard. The familiar elevated lactate signal competes with a multidomain response assessment.
authorGate.singleBestAnswer: Current observations support retaining the target. This does not certify complete recovery or discontinue serial reassessment.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Perfusion is improving, lactate is falling and stroke volume does not respond to a reversible preload change.
authorGate.residentErrorConsequence: Chasing lactate normalization through additional fluid can create avoidable volume burden.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the trend and examination and the residual lactate becomes uninterpretable. Delete the flow response and the case no longer resolves whether additional fluid is a reasonable escalation.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If refill and urine output worsened, lactate rose and a technically reliable preload test showed a strong reversible flow increase with acceptable fluid risk, a crystalloid bolus would become the best offered order.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: First node in the case. Feedback does not describe an induced high-pressure trial, arrhythmia or the next node's specific risk-benefit result.
authorGate.residualConcern: A single reassuring peripheral examination would be insufficient. The exact draft supplies serial biochemical, organ and flow observations. Independent review should assess whether all are needed.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced a uniquely cautious 'continue reassessment' key with a concrete norepinephrine order and matched it to a concrete higher-target competitor.

choices.temptation: Interpret any lactate above the reference interval as an inadequate arterial-pressure target.

inputReview.title: Validate discordant arterial pressure before titration
clarityIssues: 'The arterial pressure system has no fluid-filled zero line' is specialized setup language without an explanation of the system being described. A resident may confuse the zero-reference arrangement with the fluid-filled arterial pressure tubing itself.

The task asks 'Which assessment', but the key is an equipment correction, while the other two choices obtain new physiological measurements. A neutral next-action task or a same-stage troubleshooting option set would be clearer.

cues.phrase: Its transducer is now above the level of the right atrium / Relevel the arterial-pressure transducer to the right atrium
cues.why: The exhibit names the misplaced object and reference point; only the key repeats both and reverses the stated setup problem. A reader can match problem to correction without interpreting the pressure discrepancy.

cues.phrase: after the bed and monitoring equipment were repositioned
cues.why: This primes equipment trouble before the table; combined with the explicit transducer position, it makes the unrelated echo and venous-saturation measurements weak competitors. The chronology is legitimate, but the current choices do not test its interpretation.

fairness: For the described conventional hydrostatic arrangement, a transducer above the right atrial reference can read falsely low. Releveling and reassessment are the best offered action. No confident reversal of the physiological rule was found.

The cuff/arterial discrepancy and unchanged examination support checking measurement validity, but the stem then supplies the exact hardware error. Recognizing the already-described error and choosing its literal correction is not two independent consequential steps.

The follow-up coherently tests a different problem after the earlier target decision. Its current cuff readings and equipment findings suffice without the preceding answer. The exact capillary-refill value and alert mental status are only in the earlier node; if strict isolated display is intended, repeat those observations concisely rather than saying merely 'remain unchanged'.
suggestions: Describe the pressure setup in ordinary, unambiguous terms, retaining the physical facts required for the hydrostatic interpretation.

Compare plausible troubleshooting or immediate management actions at the same decision stage, with waveform, reference-level and repeat-pressure observations that actually distinguish them. Do not simply hide the needed transducer position.
Alternatively, retain this as an explicitly accepted basic measurement-safety item. Do not describe the present matching task as hard clinical reasoning.

authorGate.coverTheKey: All three options act on the same transducer and have comparable grammar and length. The exhibit gives two measured heights without saying that the transducer is misplaced or naming the correction. The task asks for an action, matching every option. Equipment-repositioning priming was removed.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three pressure-system troubleshooting actions before a dose change. Echo and venous sampling no longer compete with an equipment correction.
twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the relative heights as a positive hydrostatic offset and relate its direction to the arterial-versus-cuff discrepancy.
Choose physical leveling instead of another zeroing operation or an adjustment in the opposite direction before the pressure-guided dose decision.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate. Distinguishing the hydrostatic sign from an atmospheric zero error is a practical technical inference. The question does not claim difficult hemodynamic treatment selection.
authorGate.singleBestAnswer: The exact configuration and direction of the measurement discrepancy support raising the stopcock. The source directly distinguishes leveling from zeroing in this arrangement.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The conventional stopcock is 30 cm below the right-atrial reference while the arterial display is higher than repeated heart-level cuff measurements.
authorGate.residentErrorConsequence: Treating the apparent arterial hypertension can unnecessarily reduce pressure support while true pressure remains near the intended target.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the heights or configuration, neither the required physical correction nor the zeroing distinction is established. Without the simultaneous readings, the direction of the clinical measurement discrepancy is absent. The examination now stands alone.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Put the transducer at 150 cm with the same 120 cm reference and a correspondingly low arterial display despite heart-level cuff readings near the goal. Lowering the transducer becomes the best offered correction.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: The preceding PASS question and its feedback remain exact. This node repeats current alertness, extremity temperature, refill, cuff values and the MAP goal, so it requires no recalled observations.
authorGate.residualConcern: A resident familiar with transducer physics may solve it quickly. It is retained as a fair moderate acquisition problem after removing the literal problem-to-correction matching set.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Explained the system in ordinary language, replaced the assessment lead-in with an action task and replaced unrelated physiological tests with three plausible troubleshooting actions. Raw heights replace an authored statement naming the setup fault.

inputReview.title: Do not defer empirical antibiotics for a low biomarker
clarityIssues: 'After a focused diagnostic reassessment' does not specify what is reassessed or whether it introduces any meaningful delay. A rapid reassessment can occur during the current resuscitation, so the temporal alternatives are not clearly exclusive.

cues.phrase: begin the planned empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotic treatment
cues.why: 'Planned' preannounces that the treatment decision has already been made. 'Empirical' also makes waiting for organism identification sound internally inconsistent before the learner interprets infection evidence or procalcitonin.

cues.phrase: After the initial culture identification / During the current shock resuscitation
cues.why: The option set contrasts waiting for a stated pending result with the sole immediate option in an explicitly urgent shock frame. The low biomarker can be ignored and the familiar urgency rule still selects the key.

fairness: Starting empirical antibiotics during current resuscitation is clinically defensible given the infection findings, hypotension and already obtained samples. A procalcitonin result within the reference interval does not reliably exclude the need for treatment in this setting.

The vague reassessment option is the fairness problem: it can overlap with prompt treatment, rather than represent a clearly different management decision. This is repairable wording and option design, not evidence that delayed antibiotics are equally appropriate.

The presentation is short, patient-specific and self-contained. The explanation communicates the useful principle, but the current item tests one timing rule, not two consequential inferences. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: Remove 'planned' and ask a neutral, complete management task. State the actual reassessment action if it remains an option and make its relationship to starting treatment unambiguous without inventing a fixed delay.
Use a credible competing interpretation of the supplied evidence if a resident application item is desired; do not simply make infection less certain while leaving an unsupported key.
If the objective is the basic safety rule that a low procalcitonin must not delay treatment of likely infection with shock, seek explicit basic-item acceptance and keep the item short.

inputReview.title: Time source control during ongoing resuscitation

cues.phrase: The surgical and interventional-radiology teams have agreed on drainage / the agreed drainage procedure
cues.why: The indication and procedure are settled twice. In this option set, the learner is left choosing the plainly indicated intervention against two complete-recovery delays, rather than resolving a remaining procedural decision.

cues.phrase: Schedule drainage after vasopressors have been discontinued / Schedule drainage after lactate reaches the reference interval / Proceed with drainage during the ongoing resuscitation
cues.why: Two options demand complete resolution of a current abnormality, while the key is the only concurrent action and repeats the task's resuscitation language. This wait/wait/proceed structure provides an urgency shortcut.

fairness: Proceeding with drainage during ongoing resuscitation is the best offered plan. The explanation appropriately includes procedural safety assessment and does not require complete lactate normalization or vasopressor discontinuation.

The physiological observations do not distinguish close competing plans: either complete-recovery delay remains inferior over a broad range of the supplied values. Removing the lactate number and exact MAP does not change the answer. This is one source-control timing rule, not a two-step decision.

The sequence is coherent: antibiotics have begun, CT localizes a collection, and a drainage approach is agreed. The update supplies enough current information to answer independently. Earlier feedback's instruction to treat infection during resuscitation further rehearses the concurrent-treatment pattern, though it does not literally name drainage.
No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The procedure's exact technical approach need not be invented because this task explicitly concerns timing.
suggestions: Replace the two unsupported complete-recovery prerequisites with credible plans addressing an actual, explicitly described remaining safety or sequencing issue. Keep source control urgent and obtain evidence for any proposed procedural constraint.

Do not add an arbitrary waiting interval, drug threshold or organ-specific procedure comparison simply to create difficulty. If no genuine competing decision fits this objective, retain it only through explicit acceptance as a basic safety item.
Remove duplicate statements that the drainage decision is agreed while retaining enough context to keep the task about timing rather than indication.

inputReview.title: Choose the initial reassessment of persistent shock

cues.phrase: Obtain bedside transthoracic echocardiography
cues.why: Only this investigation is explicitly described as bedside, giving it a portability advantage in an unstable-patient vignette. This is a partial wording cue, not proof by itself: a pulmonary artery catheter can also be placed at the bedside.

fairness: Bedside echocardiography is the best offered first investigation. Persistent severe hypotension with elevated filling pressure and absent response to a monitored bolus warrants reassessment for cardiac or obstructive contributions. Immediate transport for targeted CT is less attractive, and an invasive catheter does not substitute for structural assessment.

The main weakness is the deletion test. The same first-echo answer follows from undifferentiated persistent severe shock even without the neck-vein, narrow-pulse-pressure and filling-pressure details. Those findings suggest a mechanism, but interpreting that mechanism is not necessary to select among the current options.

The postoperative context makes embolism a credible possibility, but the options primarily distinguish a familiar first-line test from a targeted transfer investigation and an invasive later investigation. This remains easy for the intended resident audience.
The first node is self-contained, its task is complete and the explanation does not overstate a definite obstructive diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: To require two consequential steps, supply an actual limitation or result of the initial assessment and ask for the next investigation that resolves the remaining physiological question. Give enough acquisition information to distinguish repeat or alternative imaging from advanced hemodynamic measurement or CT.
Keep option descriptions comparable in setting and specificity; do not use 'bedside' only to advertise the preferred test's feasibility.
If this remains an initial-echo recognition item, label and obtain acceptance of that basic role. Do not raise apparent difficulty by adding more classic shock findings that do not affect the choice.

authorGate.coverTheKey: No option alone is labeled bedside or immediately available. All labels are named investigations at the same next-assessment stage. The exhibit retains valid local findings without calling the entire study negative or naming the eventual diagnosis.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three next investigations after an actual incomplete acquisition. This is no longer a first-echo recognition question.
twoConsequentialSteps: Separate an adequately observed left-ventricular contraction finding from the right-sided and surrounding structures that were never visualized.
Choose an alternative acoustic approach that addresses the acquisition failure instead of enhancing one existing border or obtaining pressures without the missing structural assessment.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate to hard. The nearest error is escalating an acquisition that addresses a different limitation, or overextending the valid left-ventricular finding into whole-heart exclusion.
authorGate.singleBestAnswer: The physical acquisition limits and unexamined structures resolve the comparison in favor of TEE. Its actual use requires operator expertise and the usual safety screen, with no blanket outcome-benefit claim.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The acquisition log documents inaccessible windows and unvisualized target structures, rather than poor endocardial definition in otherwise complete images.
authorGate.residentErrorConsequence: Treating the limited study as a complete structural assessment can leave a reversible cardiac or obstructive mechanism unrecognized.
authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the acquisition details and the distinction between contrast TTE and TEE is not established. Delete the persistent pressure/filling problem and there is no stated immediate reason to pursue those unexamined structures.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If suitable transthoracic views covered the relevant structures and only ventricular endocardial definition remained inadequate, contrast-enhanced TTE would become the best offered investigation.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: The previous pericardial intervention is parked, so this revised node is a self-contained assessment. Its feedback supplies no subsequent scored answer. No future diagnosis is disclosed.
authorGate.residualConcern: The current supporting cohort is cardiovascular-ICU evidence. The acquisition principle applied to this abdominal postoperative case is an explicit physical inference requiring clinician review.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Supplied an actual initial acquisition log, retained the valid local result and compared contrast TTE, TEE and invasive hemodynamic measurement. Removed key-only portability wording. The materially changed assessment objective receives concept version 2.

observationClassification.numericBoundary: Patient measurements are constructed observations. The pressure-reference relationship is source-supported. No new clinical probability, dose, cutoff, waiting interval or demographic weight is authored.
